lines: His first product failed nine times out of ten. And that is what built the company.
Maine. Nineteen twelve. Leon Bean loves to hunt. And he is sick of wet feet.
So he has a boot made. Leather on top. Rubber on the bottom.
He mails a flyer to hunters. With a promise. Not happy? You get your money back.
He sells one hundred pairs.
Then the post starts coming back.
The stitching is tearing out of the rubber. The tops are coming clean off.
Ninety pairs. Out of one hundred. Returned.
That is the end of most businesses. He could have gone quiet. He could have blamed the customer.
He refunded every single one. It nearly finished him.
Then he fixed the boot. And mailed again.
Word got around. Not about a broken boot. About a man who kept his word.
More than a hundred years later, that company is still here. And that promise is what people know it for.
You can not fake that. How you treat people on a bad day is your reputation.
At Bluewater, we make sure it gets seen. We ask every customer for a review. And we help you answer every one.
A company promised a hundred pounds in an advert. Then a court made them pay it.
London. Eighteen ninety one. The flu is everywhere. And people are scared.
One company sells a rubber ball full of powder. Squeeze it, and breathe in the smoke.
Their advert makes a big promise. Use it three times a day, for two weeks.
If you still catch the flu, they will pay you one hundred pounds.
And to show they meant it, the advert said a thousand pounds was sitting in the bank.
Louisa Carlill reads it. She buys one. And uses it exactly as told. For about two months.
She catches the flu.
So she asks for her hundred pounds. The company ignores her. Twice.
In court, they argue it was only an advert. Not to be taken seriously.
The judges disagreed. The company had banked money to show it meant it. So it had to pay.
That was eighteen ninety two. Law students still read that case today.
A promise in an advert is still a promise.
That is why you will never hear us promise you the top spot. Or a flood of calls. Nobody honest can.
At Bluewater, we write ads you can stand behind. Every word.
To get people into his shop, he marched pigs through the middle of the city.
Glasgow. Eighteen seventy one. A young man named Thomas Lipton opens a small grocery.
Every street already has a grocer. Nobody needs another one.
So he does not put up a sign and wait.
He gets pigs. Real ones. And has them driven through the streets, straight to his door.
Carts stop. People stare. People follow.
And the message is obvious. The bacon in this shop is fresh.
Then it gets bigger. He ships in a giant cheese from America. And parades it through town.
He hides coins inside cheeses. It is reported they sold out in two hours.
Again and again, the city had something new to talk about. And it always ended at his counter.
By eighteen eighty eight, he had about three hundred shops.
Asked for the secret, he said there was no secret. Advertise all you can.
He never said, we have great prices, please come. He gave the street something to watch.
Your town still works like that. People share what is worth watching. And scroll past what is not.
At Bluewater, we make that kind of content for you. Filmed, edited and posted.
A jeweller bought twenty miles of leftover wire. And needed the police to hold back the crowd.
August, eighteen fifty eight. For the first time, a telegraph cable runs under the Atlantic Ocean.
A message can cross the sea without a ship. New York loses its mind.
Parades. Fireworks. One paper said the city had gone cable mad.
A jeweller on Broadway is watching all of it. Charles Tiffany.
Twenty miles of cable are left over, still coiled on the ship.
He buys all of it.
He cuts it into pieces four inches long. Puts a brass band round each one. With his name on it.
Fifty cents each.
One history of the company says the crowds were so big, the police had to be called.
Here is the twist. The cable itself stopped working within weeks.
But those little pieces are still in museums. With his name still on them.
He did not invent the cable. He did not lay it. He just showed up, fast, while everyone was looking.
Something is always happening in your town. A big game. The first snow. The first hot weekend.
At Bluewater, we watch for those moments. And get your business into them while they still matter.
The first package holiday cost one shilling. And it went to a meeting about not drinking.
England. Eighteen forty one. Trains are brand new. Most people have never been on one.
Thomas Cook is a cabinet maker. One day he is walking fifteen miles to a meeting. On foot.
Somewhere on that road, he has an idea.
What if he hired a whole train?
He goes to the railway. And he does the deal.
July the fifth. About five hundred people climb into open carriages.
One shilling. There and back. Tea and buns included. A band on board.
They did not have to plan anything. They did not have to understand the railway.
They just had to show up.
And he rode with them. The whole way. To make sure it went right.
By eighteen sixty five, he said he had booked a million passengers.
People did not want to learn how trains worked. They wanted to get there.
Marketing is the same. You do not want to learn ads, video, websites and reviews. You have a business to run.
That is Bluewater. One team. Everything handled. You run the business. We run the marketing.
A student made a million dollars from one web page. It sold nothing. Just dots.
England. Two thousand and five. Alex Tew is twenty one. He is about to start university. And he is broke.
He needs an idea. A big one.
Here it is. A web page with one million tiny dots. One dollar per dot.
Buy some, and you get a little picture there. Linked to your own site.
That is it. That is the whole business.
It cost him about fifty euros to set up.
His family and friends buy the first few. He spends that money telling the newspapers.
And the story is so simple, everybody repeats it. A student is selling a million dots. A dollar each.
Four and a half months later, there are only a thousand dots left.
He auctions them. Thirty eight thousand one hundred dollars.
The total. One million, thirty seven thousand, one hundred dollars.
Hundreds of people copied the page. None of the copies took off.
The page was never the clever part. You understood it in five seconds. And you knew exactly what to do.
At Bluewater, we rework websites that way. One clear idea. One clear thing to do next.
Four words changed what seven out of ten customers ordered.
New York. The nineteen thirties. Elmer Wheeler has one of the strangest jobs in America.
He stands in shops, and tests sentences on real customers. Same product. Different words. And he counts.
A big store hires him. Their soda fountain sells malted milk. An egg in it costs extra.
The clerks have been asking, would you like an egg in that?
And most people say no.
So he changes the question. And he changes one more thing.
The clerk picks up an egg in each hand. Holds them up. And asks.
One egg, or two?
It is reported that seven out of ten people took at least one.
He tested more than a hundred thousand sentences that way. And threw nearly all of them out.
His rule. Do not ask if. Ask which.
Same counter. Same eggs. Same customers. Different words.
Now look at your website. Your ads. The message you send after a quote. Did anybody test those words? Or did somebody just type them?
At Bluewater, we write them on purpose. And we keep the ones that work.
The Hollywood sign was never meant to be a landmark. It was an advert for houses. Built to last eighteen months.
Los Angeles. Nineteen twenty three. A group of developers are selling plots of land in the hills.
The estate has a name. Hollywoodland.
And they want the whole city to see it.
So telephone poles and sheet metal get dragged up the mountain. On dirt paths.
Thirteen letters. Each one about fifty feet tall.
Four thousand light bulbs. Flashing in turn. Holly. Wood. Land.
A man lived in a cabin beside it. His whole job was changing the bulbs.
It cost about twenty one thousand dollars. Just an advert. Meant to come down in a year and a half.
Then the estate went under.
But the sign stayed. In nineteen forty nine, the last four letters came down.
And the advert became one of the most famous signs on earth.
Nobody remembers the houses. Everybody knows the sign.
Most marketing vanishes the moment you stop paying for it. The good stuff stays up.
At Bluewater, we film real video of your business. The kind you can keep using for years.
One man sold thirteen thousand cars. One customer at a time. His secret weapon was a greeting card.
Detroit. Nineteen sixty three. Joe Girard is in his thirties, and flat broke.
He talks his way into a job at a car dealership.
Most salesmen sell a car, shake a hand, and that is the last the customer ever hears from them.
He does the opposite.
Every person who buys from him goes into a file.
And every single month, every one of them gets a card in the post.
New Year. Halloween. Groundhog Day. A different card every time.
With the same three words. I like you.
At his peak, he was mailing around thirteen thousand cards a month.
So when it was time for a new car, they knew exactly who to call.
Nineteen seventy three. One thousand four hundred and twenty five cars in a single year. A world record.
The trick was not talking. It was never letting a customer forget he existed.
Most businesses do the hard part. They win the customer. Then they go silent.
At Bluewater, we set up the follow up. So your past customers keep hearing from you.
A nurse changed the British Army with a drawing.
Eighteen fifty six. Florence Nightingale comes home from the Crimean War. And she is furious.
In the army hospitals, most of the soldiers who died were not killed by their wounds.
They died of disease. In dirty wards. With bad water and no fresh air.
It could have been prevented. And she had the numbers to prove it.
But she knew what happens to numbers. They go into a long report. And the report goes into a drawer.
So in eighteen fifty eight, she draws a picture.
A wheel. One wedge for every month of the war.
Red for wounds. A thin sliver.
Blue for disease that could have been prevented. Enormous.
You do not need to read a single word. You look at it, and you know.
She prints two thousand copies. And gets them in front of the people in power, and the press.
The army's hospitals were reformed. Because someone made the truth impossible to miss.
Most business owners get reports full of numbers they never read. So nothing changes.
At Bluewater, you get one clear report every month. What we did. What happened. What comes next.
